utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I asked you yesterday about an event that you raised in cross-examination in Suva Reka when you were explaining why you believe you had no trust in investigators. What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was head of the commission for the application of the Military Technical Agreement. It was a commission that was an official body of the KFOR, and I was heading our side of that commission. My opposite number in KFOR was Major Bruno Nevaj [phoen]. At one meeting we asked why in Suva Reka a mass grave had been opened at the request of The Hague Tribunal, and when the body of Milivoje Ristanovic, a Serb, was found in that mass grave, the mass grave was closed down and the whole case was closed. Following orders of General Nevaj, Sergeant Guido [phoen] answered our question. He was heading or, rather, representing the police force on the commission. He said that he couldn't see anything strange about it and wanted to know why we are interested in the issue. He said that all these mass graves are in fact cemeteries and he's confused by our question. He promised to give some more explanation but it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. According to the agreement between Ahtisaari-Chernomyrdin Agreement and the Resolution 1244, was it envisaged for the KLA to be demilitarised and disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen. The KLA just changed its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... cross-examination best identified first. It looks like a new topic but it may be not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed your point, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this relates to in cross-examination. It may do, but we need to have the topic identified for clarity, otherwise we're just going into something new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the area of the cross-examination from which this arises?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the part where Mr. Nice asked the witness why he doubted the objectivity and proper conduct of KFOR members and UNMIK members in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is it the task of the protection force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must wait until I have ruled. What is your line of questioning now in relation to Resolution 1244?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice asked the witness why he doubted the objectivity of KFOR and UNMIK in Kosovo, and I'm asking him now if, according to Resolution 1244, KFOR and UNMIK had the task of protecting the entire population in Kosovo. Was it their task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have not been asked a question. I have not yet ruled on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did they have the task of protecting the entire population of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they protect them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. Many killings and expulsions have shown that, and the 17th of March was the best evidence how they are performing their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice showed you "As Seen, As Told." Reading that book, were you able to conclude that what is written there has been seen by the authors?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never read anything like such-and-such a person saw this. I think it was just a conveniently selected title to produce an effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice showed you a footnote concerning an event involving alleged crimes, and the footnote listed about 15 witnesses. Do you think it can be taken as authentic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and do you believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to comment on. We'll make our minds up about those matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At one point Mr. Nice asked you on the basis of what you gained your insight, and he mentioned the book, the book I just referred to. My question is very specific: Did you gain your insight into the situation in Kosovo based on books or based on personal experience and firsthand knowledge and information?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija, and primarily in Djakovica, I was present most of the time. Besides, I had my command in Djakovica. There were commanding officers who had lived in Djakovica even before my arrival and before the beginning of the aggression. There were two of my battalions in Djakovica, so I had direct knowledge about the events that was not gained on the basis of books or brochures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the 24th of March. You said that on that day you were on Cabrat hill, overlooking Djakovica when the bombing began.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that something was burning in Djakovica. Why was it burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the church of St. Anthony that was on fire. You said it was in the direct vicinity of the barracks. How did it come about? Why was it burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church wasn't burning. It's a Catholic church that is right next to the barracks. It wasn't burning, and it wasn't damaged until the 11th of June when we left Djakovica. For a while, part of our medical capacities were put up in that church, and we had a very good relationship with the priests of that church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say it was not damaged during the war at all, it was damaged after our forces left?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was leaving Djakovica on the 11th of June, the church was not damaged. I know that for certain. I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was destroyed and what was burning on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Catholic Street was on fire. It's a street directly under Cabrat hill. It's almost part of Cabrat. It's a neighbourhood called Cabrat. It's an old street, lined mainly with wooden houses, very old houses dating back to the Turkish time. It is a very beautiful street but it was on fire that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of NATO bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice insisted on paramilitary units. Did you have occasion to learn about any paramilitary unit in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no paramilitary units in Djakovica, if we don't count the members of the terrorist organisation KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said several times that your evidence has to be shrunk exclusively to events concerning your unit. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were commander of the garrison, did you have insight into the situation in Djakovica as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of everything taking place in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about every major event in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... leading question, especially when the witness has by and large retracted most things he said when he himself said he knew everything about something. I don't know where this re-examination is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, have you withdrawn any of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about events in Djakovica and I questioned you after you explained you were garrison commander in Djakovica, and Mr. Bonomy also questioned you about that, should you know of an incident if it had happened as described in the materials of Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered if an event had happened, I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not a proper question. It may be a technical matter that you're unable to formulate the questions properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, I was questioning you point by point, paragraph by paragraph, about all events that happened in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for some of these things to happen, like Qerim? You explained you were in Ljug Bunar, 500 metres away, and a number of other events. So would you have known about those incidents if they had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had happened, I would have known about them because I had briefings and reports, and I said then that part of my unit was in Djakovica. I had my commanding officers in Djakovica, Nik Peraj was in Djakovica all that time, and if such a major event as the one alleged had indeed happened, I would have had to have found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions regarding your war diary. Mr. Nice said that the format differs from day-to-day. Are all the pages the same in terms of format?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in terms of size?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their size is the same. All the pages are the same, but the writing is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Every page has a number. Are they all paginated in the same handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is then the difference between pages where entries are made horizontally or vertically?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the style of the person who happened to be in command at the time and who made entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did one or more persons make entries in the diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who usually keeps that diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the operatives in the operations department or one of my deputies or assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it always the case with your diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not always the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7, a question of volunteers was mentioned. Do you have this diary in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you my copy because I have only one before me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since the witness doesn't have a copy, Mr. Robinson, can we save time if I read from that page in order to ask the witness a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the date and time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 2nd of April, 1999. It is a Friday. It says the tenth day of the war. The page is page number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please read out what it says in the middle of the page, roughly. It says 1700 hours. What does it say after that, in the line beginning with 1700?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says at 1700 hours a group of 80 volunteers arrived in the barracks of Metohija and they were deployed among the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That will suffice. Thank you. So that is the only sentence which refers to volunteers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when the volunteers arrived, were they organised into a united formation, unit, or was the procedure different?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The volunteers were always brought in by an officer from the personnel department of the corps command, and he brought them in with all their documents, their IDs, their military booklets, and everything that accompanies those. Now, on the basis of that and their age and principally where they had done their military service and what their speciality was, military speciality was, we would distribute them amongst the units. And so if somebody had done their military service, for example, as a signalsman, he would go to the signals company. If he had manned a P cannon, PA cannon, then he would go to a company where cannons were used. So there were volunteer -- some volunteers who did not have any of these special training courses but were educated people and were able to work at the headquarters, the staff, and be in charge of documentation, for example, administrative work, and so on and so forth. There were those who were infantrymen, and they were assigned to the infantry units, for example, to provide security. For the most part that is how we assigned individuals to different jobs and posts, but they were never in the same unit, all in the same Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unit, and there was not just one single unit, and he was never -- these units were never commanded by the people who came with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were distributed amongst the different units, just like any other military recruit and conscript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were in fact military conscripts but those who were not on our lists and weren't called up in a mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice showed that the 26th of April was lacking, was missing in the diary, and then Mr. Kwon said that the 26th of April does exist in the typed-out text. So would you now take a look at that date, the 26th of April. It is page 4 from -- the fourth page from the back of the copy of the diary. It's in the diary that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't find that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 26th of April. That is the day before the 27th, because Mr. Nice found it strange that that date, the 26th, was missing.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before. It's one page before the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, obviously if it's the original and since the accused has drawn to our attention that the page numbering at the top right-hand corner is in hand, it should be page number 32. Page number 32 I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's only in the typed-out version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's in the typed-out version, the story becomes even more odd, because the accused has represented to us through the Court and directly to Ms. Dicklich via one of the accused's associates that we were to be provided with and thus have been provided with everything of the original documentation that was provided to the accused. So if there's a typed-out version of this day, the 26th of April, and I'd overlooked it, it's evidence that there is more of the original document that the accused has than he's provided us, and I'd like to see it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't wish to be sidetracked by this issue but, Mr. Milosevic, can you comment on that briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the briefest possible terms and the clearest comment I can give you is to say that during the course of the day you will be provided with the entire diary. Mr. Tomanovic has informed me that the entire diary will be available in the course of today. Now, this printed page, this typed-out page is the typed-out page of the handwritten page from that missing page that Mr. Nice is missing. But once you receive the diary in its entirety, you will all be able to look through it from first to last page in the original or, rather, photocopy of the original which was in the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the sooner we get the entire diary, the better for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- of the accused's exhibits for this witness. And if Your Honours' papers are in the same format as mine, there were three -- there were originally some three parts to it; the first two, separately stapled, were in English, and if you go to the second of those two parts, if it's the same as in my papers, the second of those two parts and to the second page, you'll find an entry for the 26th of April. But it, of course, remains extremely unsatisfactory if the accused has had all the time had either all of the diary, as may be found, if he's able to produce it today, or even these relevant dates in the originals, that they weren't made available before cross-examination. And this is not, in my respectful submission, sidetrack, it's a very important issue. The production of documents like this which have simply never been available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're coming very close to imputing ill motives to the accused without any proper foundation, and I cannot sanction that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon, but I'm not doing any such thing. What I'm doing is drawing to the Court's attention, in the course of a forensic process that needs to be rigorous, first of all the extraordinary fact that documentation like this which we've sought - not these particular ones, the generality - time and time again first comes to our attention in the circumstances it does; and secondly, that the two critical dates for this witness were not made available to us until I requested them; and thirdly - and this is the point to which I was going to refer and that Your Honour will no doubt want to have in mind - there is now clearly a document, the Reka plan, which is of extreme importance, possibly, to one of the most serious and notorious events that happened in this region at the time, and it's a document we've got to get our hands on, if it exists, and before there's any question of its not being provided, whoever holds it, in its best form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we'll have to consider what to do when the diary becomes available later today by the time the -- this witness's testimony may have concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Disclosure issues between the Prosecution and the government of Serbia and Montenegro are nothing to do with this accused and Mr. Nice continually makes his complaint as though it's against the accused, but it is not an issue with which he is concerned, and that must be borne in mind. This is not a matter under his control, and therefore to make continually points against the accused on this matter is indeed unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've already said enough on that issue and I don't wish to have it commented further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I'll come back to it later today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I'm going to consult about the implications of the diary becoming available later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to draw your attention to one thing, Mr. Robinson. I received just those pages which you received yourselves. The previous selection was made by my associate with the witness, and some pages were provided by way of example. Now, since Mr. Nice insisted that the diary be produced in its entirety, as you can see it has been produced and you will be able to see whether anything -- any attempts were made to conceal something or not. And I can tell you that I didn't have any other of the pages than you did. And if I were to read the whole diary from start to finish, I don't know when I could be expected to have the time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic, is that we're getting it very late in the testimony of this witness, but we'll see what happens when we get it and then make a decision as to what course to take, if any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just let's clarify this point. You have in front you page 33 on which we find the 27th of April, which is the critical day, and yesterday you quoted what it said there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the 27th of April here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's page 33. You have the same copy of the diary that I do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my copy the pages are not numbered. I read it from the overhead projector yesterday. It was placed on the overhead projector, and I read from that. I haven't got it here before me now. Let me have a better look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In order to save time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness should have the handwritten pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the 27th, but it's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is from my diary, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says there -- or, rather, what does it say? It starts -- something started. Read out that first line, please. The 27th.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of the page, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the page. Well, not really from the beginning because there's mention of the bombing first.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak slowly, read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, you're -- just a second. Just a minute. The interpreter is asking you to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Operations are being conducted by the air force in the Devet Jugovica barracks," and then it says: "At 0600 hours an operation started to clean the Siptar terrorist forces 'Reka.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You needn't go on to explain who participates in it because that's what you do after that. So what kind of operation is that recorded there? What does that entry mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an action against the Siptar terrorist forces in the region called Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this give any possibility for broader interpretations? If we say Siptar terrorist forces, that it can relate to anybody else except to terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Exclusively to terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Nice asked you a question related to a stenogram of the Supreme Defence Council of 1995, and I used, when I intervened once, the proverb "Fear keeps the house safe." Do you know of that proverb?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite a customary, traditional proverb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what barracks were empty when the army arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the barracks were empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how old was the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started to say yesterday that the barracks dated back to 1932. The army had been there since 1932.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this proverb "Fear keeps the house safe," who was it who should have felt fear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrorists, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with the citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why should they fear anything? Why should an honest man be frightened of the army or of the police, because the barracks had been there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. Robinson. That completes my re-examination. As you can see, I kept it short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, we are considering whether, in the event that you might have questions to raise once you see the diary, we should ask the witness to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would invite you to do that, in case. And I'd invite the Court also to seek clarification from the accused of what he's explained to us. The provision of documents is, as Mr. Kay says -- he's not, I'm afraid, reflecting the reality. Provision of documents is an extremely important matter. As against the authorities, we've made it quite clear that we believe we are being obstructed and have been consistently obstructed. We have laid out before you in various ways the difficulties we have in obtaining documents and, from time to time, have suggested that there may be different standards applied to us than those applied to the accused. That may not be the accused's fault, I'm just saying that. Now, as to what he said this morning, and he said that we've had in handwritten form all that he's had, that obviously can't be right because without the provision of the handwritten version for the 26th of April, it wouldn't be possible for the 26th of April to have been transcribed and translated into English. So clearly there has been more in the possession of the accused than we've seen with this witness. If the -- the second point is that if this -- if the accused is going to be able today to provide the whole version of the diary in its original format, we'll be interested indeed in reviewing it, then either A, someone on the accused's side has had it for a long time, or B, and this is even more interesting from the Court's point of view, there is a process whereby such documentation can be found overnight. And that is of extreme value to know, because if that really is the case, then there may be more documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's wait until it happens. This debating speculatively about what might emerge is pointless. That's number one. And number two is it does appear to me Mr. Kay is quite right, that applications for documents made by the Prosecution are ex parte of the accused and therefore he isn't involved in that process. It's important to distinguish that situation from the provision by the accused of material that he does get in an entirely unsatisfactory way, in dribs and drabs, as has apparently been the case with this diary. So we mustn't confuse the two situation. You may be perfectly justified in your criticism, but it's important to get the right basis for that criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I agree with the distinction and I actually hope to keep it in mind at all times. Those the points I want to make, but immediate point is would the Chamber think it helpful to know how it is, if and when we get the original, the diary in full, how it is that it's become available not least because if it appears that there is a way of getting material in 24 hours, then we needn't -- then we should act on that basis in the future because it would be of great value to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm interested to discover, speaking for myself, Mr. Milosevic, is how soon will the diary be available today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's supposed to arrive from Belgrade, and I gave you the notification that I received from Mr. Tomanovic yesterday, namely that last week when this issue was raised, he immediately submitted a formal request, marked "urgent" since testimony was under way, to get original diary from the archives in its entirety, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and he told me earlier today that it should be arriving later today, and I suppose it's supposed to be brought by somebody who is arriving today. As soon as it's here, you will get it. Second, as to what Mr. Nice said, that I had a typed-out page and that that is proof that I had had a manuscript page, that would have been true only if I were the person who types things out, which is not the case. I get typed-out pages just as you do. There is no intent to withhold portions of the diary behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General Djosan, that concludes your testimony, but in view of the developments, we are asking you to remain today and to make yourself available for tomorrow morning in the event that it might be necessary to ask you further questions arising from the examination of the diary which will be received later today. So you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I call my next witness, I should like to raise an administrative issue and to provide you with a piece of information. May I do this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It won't take more than two minutes. You informed me, Mr. Robinson, that I have received a confidential Prosecution witness list, something the Registry provided by day of testimony during the Prosecution case. That's what the Registry provided. And this practically consists of two documents. One relates to the Kosovo stage, which began on the 12th of February, 2000, and the other one relates to Croatia and Bosnia stage that began on the 26th of September, 2002. I suppose you received the same documents. At least, I hope so. From these documents, one can see that, by dates contained therein, there is a total of 279 days of the Prosecution case. I suppose the difference to the total --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not hearing that now. I'm not hearing any submissions on that issue now. Call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Robinson, I will be done in 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's out of order. It's out of order, entirely out of order. Had I known that was the purpose of the request for you to intervene on an administrative matter, I would not have allowed it. I'm not hearing it. Call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can you tell me when you will be hearing this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any submission you have on that issue should be put in writing. Call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I'm going to call the next witness. I just want to say that the hours are missing amounting to at least 70 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I cut you off, Mr. Milosevic, because that's a flagrant abuse of the ruling that I made. Call your next witness if you have one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth -- excuse me. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may commence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but the volume is very low in my headphones. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may commence, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if the map of Kosovo could be put up behind the witness so that he can show us his area of responsibility to begin with. We will start, in the meantime, while it's being done, to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, would you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vlatko Vukovic. I was born on the 15th of August, 1960, in Mramor village. It's a very small village in the municipality of Kovin in the autonomous province of Vojvodina in Serbia. I was born to a family of workers. My father's name is Momir; mother's name Stana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe your career briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Military academy of the ground forces, which I completed in 1983. My first place of service was the garrison of Pirot, in which I occupied initial duties, as an officer, of course. In 1988, I was transferred to the academy of ground forces of Yugoslavia, where I acted as a commander and lecturer. In 1998, I was transferred to the Djakovica garrison. I had certain duties in Medvedja, Leskovac garrisons also, then in Belgrade as well, and in 2002 I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you served during the war in Kosovo, and could you show us your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in Kosovo and Metohija, I was commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade. I'm sorry, I'm having a hard time with this because I have a problem with my legs. The battalion that I commanded was south of Djakovica. I can tell you precisely if you need to know the borders, the boundaries of the area of responsibility of my battalion. It was Belaja river on the west; Cafavanas [phoen] pass on the south, the state border from Cafavanas pass to the Mount Pastrik; on the east from Pastrik mountain to Beli Drim river; and on the north, Beli Drim River --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And another river that the interpreter did not catch the name of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, if I understood you correctly, before the war you were in perfectly good health?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in perfectly good health, Mr. Milosevic, and I was even a good athlete. I loved sports and was very active because my service allowed me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you have serious health problems; walking, speech.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's perfectly obvious and I take this opportunity to apologise to the Trial Chamber and the interpreters as well, because sometimes I swallow an entire word or a syllable. My condition first occurred during the war, in 1999. Unfortunately, our doctors do not deal with causes. They only deal with consequences, and they only treat consequences and symptoms. I must say that after full six years, they haven't been able to give a precise diagnosis, but it may be the use of all sorts of weapons and materiel during the NATO bombing of my country. And generally speaking, this area south of Djakovica is marked on all maps as the area with the densest number of various projectiles that fell, projectiles carrying depleted uranium and other material that cause evaporations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand. Did you say that -- did you say that the illness which you have, your medical condition, was in some way associated with weapons and materiel during the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can say that safely, because I know that before the bombing I was in perfectly good health and fully able, whereas on the 14th or the 15th of June that year, after just three months, I was a serious invalid. I weighed 54 kilos, and I had trouble, serious trouble, walking and talking. I am now much better than I was at that time. So I do link it exclusively to the use of NATO weapons and materiel in the aggression against my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's your speech and your gait that are affected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my speech and my gait. That is the most noticeable part. However, there are many other things. I have poor coordination and I'm not very stable on my feet. I have trouble swallowing. I don't want to go into all the details now, but, yes, speech and gait are the two most adverse consequences and most noticeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what sports were you involved prior to your illness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All kinds of sports that you would expect an army officer to engage in. I was also a ski instructor, a swimming instructor, and all the other sports; athletics, sports with balls, et cetera, ball games and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, we're now going to go on to specific places within your area of responsibility, and let's start with the municipality of Orahovac. We introduced an exhibit here that General Delic testified about. It was the order for the support of MUP to destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Orahovac, Suva Reka, Velika Krusa, and that was compiled on the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you have that document in your list. It is tab 356, used on the 30th of June this year, and it was admitted into evidence on the 1st of July. So it is an exhibit. It has been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you act upon that order and what did this document mean to you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order. I've looked through it. It is an order by the corps commander for support and reinforcement to MUP forces to destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Velika Krusa, as it says. Of course, pursuant to this order and generally speaking, the law provided for the fact that each unit and each individual must act within the spirit of the order given by their superior command. That means that I acted and my unit acted in this operation exclusively pursuant to the order received from my superior command. And I can briefly comment this order if need be. You tell me if I need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. We're not going to comment on that order now because it is very precise and was commented on by General Delic in his testimony. And during that testimony, it was admitted into evidence, so it is entitled "Order for the destruction of the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Retimlje and the block Suva Reka and Orahovac and control of the territory," and that was brought in by General Delic himself, and that is to be found under number 3, and it is D300, tab 357, and it was admitted into evidence, as I said, on the 1st of July, Mr. Robinson. Now, what does this document mean? Did you act upon it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this was the basic document and starting document on the basis of which, among other things, I was able to view the role and place of my own unit in this anti-terrorist operation. Of course, I was able to see the place and role of the neighbours and everything that a command would do once it receives an assignment and orders. So on the basis of this order, I was able to assess and size up the overall situation and make the decision to engage part of my unit in the operation. If you take a look at point 5, point 5 on page 3, for example, it says there Combat Group 2, 549th Motorised Brigade, and then it lists the composition of the forces engaged. That means in that operation I engaged 186 men and materiel and technical equipment. And then it says the assignment is to launch an energetic search of the village Kosa Brod, trig 342 and trig 440, and together with the forces in the blockade, to destroy the Siptar forces in Celine, Nogavac, to cut off the area of Velika Krusa, and part of the forces should be directed towards Amovac, and if the need arises, to have wing action use the flank forces in order to take control of the village of Brestovac and the village of Mala Hoca. To reinforce the platoon 122 millimetres, the command post at trig 440. That means that on the basis of an assignment of this kind that we received and the overall order, the order of -- in its entirety which came to us from the brigade command, I decided to proceed in a manner which I will describe to you later on, and to engage my forces. I should also like to draw your attention, with the Court's permission, to focus on a few other points which are a component part of every combat document and combat order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- order for combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for Mr. Milosevic to put another question. We have had a sufficiently long narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained to us what this document means and meant to you. It was a direct order which you acted upon; is that right? Is that what the explanation you gave?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is a direct order upon which all the units acted, including my own. And my decision could not have been any different from what was specified in the assignment given to us from -- by the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything that relates to you especially that is characteristic in this order?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. No characteristic traits. The rest of the document relates to all the units which are engaged. I can pinpoint certain sections if you wish me to do so and go into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's no need to go into the details of it. The essence and crux of the matter is that you acted upon the order received. Now, on the map, if we look at the map, does that reflect the order? And the number is 358 there. It was an exhibit that was admitted into evidence on the 1st of July, as I said. It's a map. Tell us what the map represents. You have it before you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is the decision of the brigade commander for this particular operation. Of course, the decision coincides with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decision made in the order itself and expressed in the order itself. And in principle, following recommendations and instructions, we indicate the initial deployment of forces before the operation goes ahead and the plan of the operation itself as conceived. Of course, it includes the positions of the troops and the positions of the Siptar terrorist forces. And here you'll be able to notice the red and green lines which represents our forces. What I'm pointing to now, that is the combat group, Combat Group 2, which I commanded. So from the crossroads here, from the village of Bela Crkva towards the Celine village via trig 340 and 440, and the other trigs 430 toward Buna Amovac. That was the line, the axis that I was assigned to establish a blockade, and it is from that line that we moved into operation, that is to say to search the terrain. That was our assignment, to search the terrain along that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, how this operation evolved. You showed us on the map -- actually, you said that the map was contemporaneous with the operation and the order for the operation.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the original decision of the commander of the 549th Brigade, and we can see in the lower right-hand corner you have his signature there. And that is a map which was a component part of the order issued, the order we discussed a moment ago. If you want to ask me about the operation itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now whether you proceeded according to the order given, and could you explain to us what your subordinates did, how they acted.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I explained a moment ago that I acted in full conformity with the order and assignment issued, the assignment and decision, and of course the assignments and tasks that are issued in the field depending on how the situation develops. It is normal and customary that I and my subordinates had to act within the spirit of the order that -- orders that I issued, and that is how every army and military organisation functions, as indeed any serious organisation; that there is one person in command and the others are there to execute that command and listen to orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the operation, were there any excessive situations which were not in conformity with the orders issued, either by your superiors or by you personally?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. During this particular operation there were no situations of that kind, and I'd like to say that the operation did follow the ideas of the commander largely speaking, especially on the first day. We sized up the situation very well, we collected information about the deployment and strength of the terrorists, and throughout the operation the chain of command was adhered to. There was no lack of discipline which would jeopardise the fulfillment of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the next document, which is D300 of tab 350, once again introduced into evidence on the 1st of July, we have an analysis compiled by General Delic. This analysis, which has to do with the destruction of Siptar forces in Retimlje and a blockade of the Suva Reka-Orahovac communication lines, as this has been set out here and described, does it correspond with your knowledge of the situation; and if not, where do the differences lie?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This corresponds fully, to my knowledge. Otherwise, an analysis of every assignment carried out, including the one we're discussing now, is done on the basis of a report by the subordinate commands, and one of those subordinate commands --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm trying to track the documents. This may be tab 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you can see from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that's what I said, the D number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, an analysis is the document which is compiled first and foremost on the basis of reports received from commanders of all the units participating. In this specific case, it is an anti-terrorist operation, and what the commander himself, the brigade commander himself, the knowledge he has gained. So that the analysis is a reflection of everything that the 549th Brigade units did over those four days in that particular area on that terrain. And I participated in compiling the analysis myself, so I'm able to say that with absolute assurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Bela Crkva is in the Orahovac municipality. Now, your movements in Bela Crkva - and let me say that Bela Crkva has been mentioned here. It is one of the places that are mentioned -- that have been mentioned here on many occasions, but Bela Crkva is in the Orahovac municipality. So your movements in Bela Crkva, were they part of the operation that you have described to us?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. My unit was, on the 25th, for a brief time in Bela Crkva as well within the frameworks of an assignment, a Combat Group 2, and I can demonstrate this on the map if you like. I don't think it's necessary, though. But anyway, from the area of deployment in the Zur village, Djakovica and Zrze and Bela Crkva, those villages and that general area, there was a march which started at one hour after midnight, 1.00 a.m., through Bela Crkva. We had to pass through Bela Crkva in order to cut off the blockade lines. So that the operation in Bela Crkva, if that's what you're asking me, and the movements in Bela Crkva are a component part of the operation we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the next piece -- exhibit, you have D30 and tab 360 is a map of Bela Crkva itself. It has already been exhibited. May it be placed on the overhead projector now, please. There you have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, here you can see the deployment of my forces, that is to say Combat Group 2, at 0430 hours, roughly. We were in the Seros [phoen] region here, right up at the border in Zrze village, and that is where I received information from my security commander at the head that in the -- everything was quiet in the village of Bela Crkva. However, he had already passed through the village and set up security on the eastern slopes of the Bela Crkva area. He informed me that in the village of Bela Crkva there was no movement whatsoever, that it was completely calm and that nobody was doing any shooting and that one police unit had already entered the western part of the village and that the unit can safely pass through up to the blockade line. While passing through the village of Bela Crkva, Combat Group 2 marched through using motorised vehicles, we were in motorised vehicles. We did not get out of the vehicles, and we passed by in a column towards the blockade line, and a portion of our forces went towards Brnjaca and then joined up at the blockade line following their own axis. We can see that at 0600 hours Combat Group 2 had set up positions along the blockade line and was ready to carry out the assignment ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you have just explained, is that contained in your report about what had happened, and who do you submit it to? So you passed through a peaceful Bela Crkva. You said you went through in a motorcade without stopping, there were no incidents, you set up a blockade line and went on.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after taking up positions on the line of blockade, it was my duty to report to my superior officer. Military reports of that kind are very brief. I said that I performed a march, that I passed through Bela Crkva without fighting, that I emerged on the line of blockade and took up positions unhindered, that I am on my command post and that I am ready to perform my assignment. It's a brief report that you make through communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In March -- in January 2003, you made a statement to the Commission for Cooperation that existed at the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, the last question, which is clearly leading in form, probably does need exploration because it's suggesting that there's an existence of a report. I don't know whether I missed it in earlier answers, but it says: "What you have explained, is that contained in your report about what happened, and who do you submit it to?" I'm not sure whether we've covered that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: His answer is that was his duty to report to a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as you know, there's a question of contemporaneity of documents or otherwise, and I'm simply not sure what's being suggested by the accused there, as it comes in leading format. It might pass into the record and be interpreted at a later stage as suggesting something that hasn't been explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the witness said the analysis -- well, that he personally participated in compiling the analysis, so I assumed he was referring to that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he's referring to that, then, that's fine. Well, if he's referring to that, I understand it better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness said that he submitted his report when he passed through and when he had taken up positions, to the brigade commander in the event, General Delic, saying that he had completed that part of the task. He said his report was brief and soldierly through communications equipment. That's what he said, his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is -- if there is separate report, where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I don't know if you noted what the witness said. He said he made the report briefly in a soldierly way, through communications equipment, to his brigade commander. So it was an oral report, as is commonly done in such situations. He's maybe communicating a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, in January 2003, you wrote a statement to the commission about your knowledge of alleged crimes in Bela Crkva village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been exhibited here during the testimony of General Delic, but I was unable to establish precisely in what way. The statement was used here, but I don't think you actually admitted it into evidence because it was not a statement of General Delic, it was the statement of this witness. Now that this witness is here -- it's D300, tab 362. It's something that you have already dealt with, you've had occasion to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO. It has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know it was marked for identification, but I would like to tender it now. It says here, "Translation provided 1st of July."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statement that I gave to the Commission for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, or more precisely, to the expert team of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the contents of this statement, as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the heading -- in the beginning I write which duties I occupied and when. I indicate the time when part of my unit participated in the blockade and search of terrain on the axis that I referred to earlier. I indicate the composition of Combat Group 2 that was established to perform this assignment. I indicate the time when the assignment was received, the objective of the anti-terrorist operation, copied from the order of the brigade commander, of course. And then in the fifth paragraph we see when Combat Group 2 set out to perform this mission, how the march was carried out. The statement is rather more detailed than my earlier description. We can see from the statement that the Combat Group 2 passed through village Bela Crkva in their motor vehicles from 5.00 to 5.30. That is very briefly. We did not notice anything in that village. There was no activity in the village. And at 6.30, we already started performing the assignment; searching the terrain and supporting police units in detecting and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you carry out a search of Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have already said there was no search in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I ask you is it is one of the assignments you have, according to the order in front of us, was to search Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The search of Bela Crkva was not carried out, because I said that my lead security, forward security, whose assignment is to ensure unhindered march for my combat group on their axis of movement, established through reconnaissance that there was no activity from Bela Crkva village against our troops. Since there was no activity against us, there was no reason for us to counteract. Counteract against whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second, we had contact with the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the search of the terrain was not conducted because there was no action coming from that terrain.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Search of terrain, Mr. Milosevic, is, incidentally, one of the most difficult and most complex military operations. If it's compounded by terrorist action, it is the most complex operation that can be performed by a unit or organised by a commander. There is no sense by exhausting your men, making them search the terrain if you have reliable information there are no terrorists there. We never did that, either in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1998 and especially not in 1999. Let me just remind you that around 2000 hours on the 24th of March, the day before, the aggression of NATO forces against our country had begun. So it was far from my mind to engage in marginal matters. Instead, we followed orders. We set out to uncover, destroy terrorist forces, and free certain roads that had been occupied by terrorists, roads that were extremely important primarily for the supply of VJ units but also for supplying the civilian population and everybody who lived in Kosovo and Metohija normally in our area, Djakovica, Prizren, and Orahovac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you can see, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, in the indictment, paragraph 56(b) -- or 66(b), it says that on the 25th of March - that is the date that you were talking about - forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded and attacked the village of Bela Crkva, Orahovac. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that this is absolutely not correct. If we go back to that map of Bela Crkva, we will see that the village of Bela Crkva had never been surrounded. And again I say there was no need to surround it. I'm talking about the original map of Colonel Delic, commander of the 549th Brigade, which constitutes the order to combat Siptar terrorist forces. On that map we see that Bela Crkva village is completely outside the area of conduct of military operations. So this is absolutely incorrect. We never surrounded Bela Crkva village, and we never performed any operations in it because there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say in the same paragraph that: "Many residents of Bela Crkva fled along the Belaja river outside the village and were forced to seek shelter near a railroad bridge. And as the forces of the FRY of Serbia -- and Serbia approached the bridge, they opened fire on a number of villagers, killing 12 persons including 10 women and children." Since you were there, what can you tell us about what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is absolutely untrue, so it's difficult to comment. But I'm looking at this allegation. This Belaja brook, it's very short. It starts in Bela Crkva from the confluence of two streams, one from east, one from west, and they make up this Belaja brook. These residents had no one to flee from, and I guarantee they didn't flee. And if they had fled along the Belaja river, they would have been going north. And if you look at the map, to the north of Belaja river there is no railroad. The railroad is south of the village. So the person who provided data for this indictment got it all wrong. These allegations are completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness says that Bela Crkva was never surrounded. The Bela Crkva village is completely outside the area of conduct of military operations. Is that -- is that the reason why you say it was never surrounded, because it was outside the area of conduct of military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, as soon as it is outside the area of conduct of combat operations, it couldn't have been surrounded. And I just explained a moment ago the activities of my unit in Bela Crkva village. We passed through in a marching column -- or, rather, motorcade. The troops were loaded onto vehicles. There were other vehicles and military equipment in the motorcade. And we passed unhindered through the village. I don't know which other words to use to explain this. In Bela Crkva village, there was absolutely no action. There was no need to surround the village. I don't see any sense in it. Why would we surround a village without it being followed by some action? That's what I'm trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph it is also alleged that: "The forces of the FRY and Serbia ordered men and older boys to strip and then systematically robbed them of all valuables. They were ordered to go back to the riverbed and later opened fire on those men and older boys, killing approximately 65." What can you say about these allegations? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say these allegations are completely untrue. I know nothing about any of this for one simple reason: This never happened. That's what I'm telling you. I was personally present there at the head of my unit, and I had absolutely all the information about things that happened not only in Bela Crkva village but in the entire area of conduct of operations. I cannot accept that the army robbed or killed and whatever is said here. That is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a Prosecution witness Isut Zhuniqi from Bela Crkva testified here that 16 policemen opened fire at 13 Kosovo Albanian civilians who were between the bridge and the police, about 50 metres away from him, the witness. He testified here on the 6th of June, 2002. It's on transcript page 6439. So 16 policemen opened fire at 13 Kosovo Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said what I had to say. It seems that the witness's testimony is the same as the indictment. I cannot comment upon something that I know never happened for certain. I would like to see a proper piece of evidence rather than such witness statements that would corroborate this. I absolutely reject the kind of statement you are presenting me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this statement that we just looked at, the statement that you provided and commented upon, you said in the last paragraph concerning alleged crimes on the 25th of March: "I first heard in late 2001 and read about it in the book 'As Seen, As Told.'" And you maintain that no crime had been committed nor had there been any combat operations conducted. You are also not aware of any crimes committed by other units.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've just explained that, and that's the conclusion of my statement. Incidentally, the statement was asked of me not only in relation to Bela Crkva. I wrote a total of ten to 15 statements where the expert team of this Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY wanted me to clarify certain points that were unclear and that were subject to differing interpretation of events in which my unit was involved. That's why I gave those statements to the commission. At the time I gave these statements, I had already been retired for quite a while. And this last paragraph confirms all that I wrote in the entirety of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you gave us a detailed explanation about Bela Crkva. You were personally present in Nogavac during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Part of my unit and myself went to Nogavac, performing an action on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the map that is marked Nogavac TK50? It was introduced during the testimony of General Delic and admitted D300, tab 433. You have it under number 8. Was it precisely your unit that was in Nogavac?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, here in the heading you see the 1st and 2nd of April. Let me just remind you: Part of my unit from trig point 339 performed actions on the axis of Nogavac and later on Randubrava, but you will notice that on the 1st of April there were no units of ours in this area. And as far as I can see, this is an indication of NATO Air Force action. It says 2nd April at 4.00 in the morning. So there was an airstrike. NATO Air Forces targeted civilians who were hesitating whether to leave the village or not. And they probably wanted to give them an impetus to flee the village. This is my assumption, it's not based on any documents. What I do know is that the police -- or, rather, during that period of time I was towards the north to continue the anti-terrorist operation, and part of the terrorists succeeded in pulling out and reaching Mount Milanovac and link up with the forces, the terrorist forces who were active up there. So after this action, an anti-terrorist operation was continued along the Orahovac-Malisevo axis, and so on and so forth. So on the 1st and 2nd I was not in Nogavac but I do know about the event and I know for sure that this action was done by NATO planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. However, here in paragraph 63(i), we see that on the 25th of March, 1999, a large group of Kosovo Albanians went to a mountain near the village of Nogavac, also in Orahovac municipality, seeking safety from attacks on nearby villages. That is what is stated. Can you comment? Can you tell us what happened there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me say that this is not at all correct, and let me tell you why. Here's why: What it says here is went to a mountain near the village of Nogavac. Mr. Milosevic, you learn in primary school that up to 500 metres is manoeuvre terrain and over 500 metres is where the mountain begins. I'd like somebody to find you on anybody's map, whichever map you like, where in the vicinity of Nogavac village there is a feature of 500 metres or an altitude higher than 500 metres. And not to waste your time, I'll tell you. The first nearest mountain is Milanovac mountain, and it is at a distance from Nogavac of some ten kilometres. Then there are mountains south across the Beli Drim River, Pastrik and so on. I don't want to enumerate them all. So this is quite incorrect. It's wrong that near the village of Nogavac there is any kind of mountain whatsoever. And then the following assertion is also incorrect, that the army attacked nearby villages. The army did not attack a single village, and I claim that with full responsibility. Just from the villages, all that -- from those places from which the Siptar terrorists opened fire on army units and soldiers did the army respond when they uncovered a fire target, which is quite normal. And this is provided for by all the rules of combat for the engagement of an army. I don't think that is characteristic only for the army of Yugoslavia. Any army would do that, and that all armies, all armed forces from all countries have the same rules and regulations as to when they engage. So what is alleged here in the indictment is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But mention is made here that the forces of FRY and Serbia surrounded these people. They surrounded them. It says they went to a mountain near the village of Nogavac in Orahovac municipality, seeking safety from attacks on nearby villages. And then it is claimed that: "Forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded them and on the following day ordered the 8.000 people who had sought shelter on the mountain to leave. The Kosovo Albanians were forced to go to a nearby school and then they were forcibly dispersed into nearby villages."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is quite incorrect. The truth of it is this: On the 26th, in this area here, in the Sap [phoen] feature, I was informed by one of my platoon commanders as soon as it was daybreak that we should -- this is a depression here, Niskovlaz [phoen], with a shrubbery, and according to his estimate - he didn't control or number them - but according to his estimate, he thought there were about 500 civilians there. Now, as since 7.00 a.m. we were supposed to carry on searching the terrain, or they were searching the terrain, he asked what should be done, and he personally took three soldiers with him, only three soldiers, and went up to those civilians and asked them where they were from, what they were doing in the area, and so on. And then he used our communication lines to inform me about it and I issued him an order and told him that since the civilians had said that they were from Celine and part of them were from the village of Nogavac, that quite simply he should pull them outside the area of combat operations, where we were expecting to engage with the terrorists and where in the Randubrava village, where the terrorists were, to pull them out and to have them return to their villages because there would be no more action in the villages. There were no more terrorists there and therefore no more action. And that was what was actually done, because the combat group commander informed me later on that the civilians had passed his positions and went on to the village of Celine. Some said they were going on further to Bela Crkva, and I think that a smaller number went to stay with relatives and another part went to Velika Krusa. So it's quite normal that the civilians should be pulled out of an area where we expect action. And this figure of 8.000 people is absolutely incorrect, just not true. As I said, we didn't count them, we didn't control the -- we didn't look at their identity cards, identity papers, but there certainly could not have been 8.000 people. And furthermore, it says they were forcibly dispersed. That is just not true. Who in their right mind -- if you were a civilian, I mean, civilians -- get away from an area where their lives would be in jeopardy, their lives and the lives their children? And let me just remind you: These groups of civilians -- or this group of civilians was, first of all, made up by women, children, and elderly males who were not military fit, fit for military service. And it is quite logical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness tends to give answers that are too long, and I'd like you to ask questions and for the witness to answer more briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, in case anybody has difficulty making easy sense of it on subsequent reading, we've been referring not to 63(i) but to 63 subparagraph (a)(i).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Who in their right mind would not get away from an area ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is (i) and it says (i). Otherwise, a Roman numeral does not have the dot above it. But I do agree it is 63, paragraph 63(a)(i).

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a very sweeping assertion, Colonel, if I can use the term, and that is why I have to ask you to pay attention to all the details. It says clearly the following: "On the 25th of March, 1999, a large group --" that's the paragraph I'm referring to, (i), paragraph 63(a)(i): Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
