"... a large group of Kosovo Albanians went to a mountain near the village of Nogavac ..." And you said a moment ago how far the mountains are from the village of Nogavac. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ten to 12 kilometres. You can see that if you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. "... seeking safety from attacks on nearby villages. Forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded them and on the following day ordered the 8.000 people who had sought shelter on the mountain to leave."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat it again and explain again: My blockade stretched from the eastern regions of Bela Crkva towards the town of Orahovac and south-east of Orahovac. Even if these civilians wanted to flee to the mountains, they would have to come across our forces that had set up a blockade. But I state once again: They could not physically have reached a mountain. That's the first point. Secondly, the army never surrounded any civilians. There was no need for them to do so. Why would they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This says here about these 8.000 people that they were forced to go to the nearby schoolhouse and then dispersed -- nearby school and then they were forcibly dispersed.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I tell you they were outside an inhabited area, a settlement. This is Sara, which is a depression, and if you look at the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the free estimation of that commander was about 500. He said there were roughly 500. So this figure of 8.000 just doesn't stand. But if you look at this area, there is no school there. A school exists in Velika Krusa, in Mala Krusa, and in Celine. But there's two kilometres. So when you say "nearby school," that must have been close to the people where -- close to the area where we had allegedly surrounded them. So you can see that this portion of the indictment just does not correspond to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on it goes on to say: "After three or four days, forces of FRY and Serbia entered the villages, went from house to house and ordered people out."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just don't know how to interpret this or explain it. Why would we send them back to the houses if we wanted to order them out again? I don't see any logic there. There's no sound logic there. So this is nonsensical, and it's very difficult for me to comment on nonsensical assertions of that kind except to say that it is absolutely not true, not correct. I was present there myself. I know that the army never surrounded civilians. I know that the army did not forcibly expel anyone, and I know that it's just not true, and I won't accept that, and I cannot accept this. I know that the army of Yugoslavia did not engage in things like this, and I was an officer of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just to be clear, in relation to this paragraph in the indictment and the previous one which dealt with Orahovac, your case is that these incidents as alleged in the indictment never took place at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have the commander of the combat group which was there on the terrain, in the field, and that's what I'm asking him about. And you heard his answer. You heard what he said. Colonel Vukovic is talking about what actually happened there, and you heard what he had to say about what it says here in the indictment; that it is a lie. It's false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says they forced them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not saying that the incidents took place but took place in a different manner than what is alleged in the indictment, you're saying they never took place at all, they never happened. I'm just asking you now what your case is, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That it never happened. That's what I learnt, and I can only learn that from the witness. He was in command. He was the commander of the units which were precisely located in that area at that time, and we're talking about the 25 of March, 1999. That's the date. That's the date stipulated here in the indictment. On that date was when the witness was there and his unit, his combat group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "Later on they forced them into the houses again and told them not to leave. Those who were not able to fit in the houses had to stay in the cars and tractors that were parked nearby." Did you see any civilians, cars, tractors?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The people who I encountered were on foot. They were only walking. There were no columns, no tractors, no motor vehicles. Quite simply, as I say, this is just not true. There is not a single piece of evidence that anything like that took place. Had there been something like that, then I would have had information about it. And the army is based on orders and the execution of orders and reporting back once those orders had been carried out. That's how an army works, functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry to have to persist and tax you here, but this is what is explained in paragraph 33. It says: "On the 2nd of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia started shelling the villages, killing a number of people who had been sleeping in tractors and cars."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Here this is partly true, but you know what part? Let me explain to you. In one part, and I've already said it, actually, earlier on. Let me take you back to the map of Nogavac, showing Nogavac. On the 2nd of April and the 1st of April and already on the 25th from 1800 hours, there was no army, no soldiers in the vicinity of the village of Nogavac at all. The army, therefore, could not, even had it wanted to, it could not have shelled them. It wasn't there. And most probably those villagers had prepared to leave Kosovo and Metohija. First of all, in the night between the 1st and 2nd of April was when the NATO Air Force targeted civilians intentionally, I say, to get them on the move, to get them moving. Not only them but all the other villagers too. And as far as I am informed, and I am indeed informed, that's where a horrendous crime took place against the civilian population during the NATO bombing. Of course, in order to trigger a humanitarian catastrophe in order to justify the aggression, which is an act of -- a criminal act according to all international rules and regulations. But it is not true that the army shelled. That was the consequence of the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 2nd of April there were no soldiers in the area, was no army there. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this area bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the area was bombed by NATO then, and I know that the civilian organs, the investigating judge conducted an on-site investigation, and so on and so forth. Of course, these inhabitants, the villagers were first helped by a police unit, a police unit that happened to be stationed in Velika Krusa and had the assignment to ensure secure -- communication and the roads between Prizren and Djakovica. They were the first people to arrive to help them and transport them to the hospital in Prizren since Prizren was the nearest town with a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, a witness of the Prosecution, Ali Hoti, said here in this room that he believes that on the 1st of April the Serb planes dropped bombs on Nogavac. What can you say about that, about that allegation? And he testified on the 22nd of April, 2002. The transcript page is 3589.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What I can say is this: That is completely incorrect, because at that time already our planes weren't flying. There was -- NATO had full air control of the airspace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So everything that I have read out to you, you say that there were none of our forces there and NATO planes were flying.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I know for sure. There were none of our forces there and on the basis of that I state that all airstrikes against the civilian population was intentional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that will suffice as far as these allegations and this portion of the indictment is concerned about -- which refers to Nogavac. Now, during the war did you participate in any activities in Mala and Velika Krusa?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, part of my unit, a platoon, passed along the fringes of Velika Krusa. The outskirts. It wasn't involved in any direct action so it was moving along the following axis: Along the Celine road towards this area here and feature 440 -- 450, sorry. And action in Velika Krusa was directed against the units and forces of the Ministry of the Interior, who were there searching the terrain. I can speak to those events if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can. We have a map here marked as Mala Krusa TK25 of the 26th of March, 1999. And we have a map of Velika Krusa dated the 25th of March. They have been admitted into evidence D300, tab 430. They have already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I move on, you said the statement of Colonel Vukovic was introduced during the testimony of General Delic and marked for identification. I would like to tender it now because Colonel Vukovic has just commented upon his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, you remember what I just said, I hope, about the maps of Mala Krusa and Velika Krusa that you have under tabs 9 and 10 in your documents, Exhibit D300, tab 430, admitted in July of this year. Can you put these maps on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: First we've got the map of Mala Krusa that deals with the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can deal with them in that sequence, or you can change the sequence.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is better for the Trial Chamber. Do you want me to deal with them in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, as briefly as possible, explain what happened in Mala and Velika Krusa.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We have to look at them comparatively to deal with the entire action. Around 7.00 on the 25th of March, the search of terrain began. The first feature on which fire was opened was precisely Velika Krusa and the wine cellar in Mala Krusa. Terrorists opened fire as the units were arriving at their initial positions. Let me tell you at the outset that Velika Krusa and Celine village are connected. There is no clearly defined border between the villages. Already at 7.30 action began, fire began from well-prepared trenches, bunkers and communicating trenches against police from Celine village on my left wing -- sorry right wing. And because the police units were stopped before Celine village - the terrorist action was very strong - the movement of my unit was slowed down. I informed my superior commander, I got additional assignments from him, and the action continued. Here again you can see that the deployment of police forces at 1200 hours is this, and the deployment of my units in yellow. You can see that until 1200 hours, search of Celine village had been completed, as well as search of Velika Krusa, and preparations were made for continued action. As for this other map of Mala Krusa, I have already said that for Combat Group 1 and the blocking forces, already during the deployment of forces fire was opened from the wine cellar area. There was also fire from Pirane, but you're now asking me about Mala and Velika Krusa. And since our units had performed their nearest task, smaller forces of the MUP remained in Mala and Velika Krusa with the exclusive assignment of securing the Prizren-Djakovica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During that operation, was there any action vis-a-vis the civilians on your part or on the part of the police units with whom you acted in coordination?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no action vis-a-vis the civilians, which is quite normal. In most cases - in fact, I can say safely say always - civilians got away from any area where they thought there might be action. Concerning Celine village, we did not have precise information because we had lost so much time during the day. Not a single artillery projectile fell on Celine or Velika Krusa, because I was the only one who had 120-millimetre gun that could perform such an action. But we didn't use 120-millimetre mortar because precisely we were not sure whether there were any civilians in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was fire at you from Celine village, but you were not sure it was empty of civilians so you didn't want to shoot?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We opted to destroy those firing points through manoeuvre and smaller calibres to avoid adverse consequences for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you report these events to your superiors, that is the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. We were all part of one communication system, and whenever there is something important to report to your superior commander, or something that may affect another unit, or if assistance is maybe needed somewhere, I report it. I may even decide to report things on my own initiative. We were permanently within this communication system, and I kept them informed about the course of this anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are now talking about your unit. What is -- what was the ethnic structure of your unit? I'm talking about commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as soldiers are concerned, it was the same as other units: In addition to Serbs, there were a lot of Muslims, quite a lot of Hungarians, quite a lot of Roma from Kosovo and Metohija, the Gorani, Turks as well, Czechs, Ruthenians; all able-bodied men fit for military service who had received their call-up papers. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And as for the ethnic structure of commanders, it was rather variegated. I can tell you the names, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It would be interesting to me. Could you please try.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the 1st company at that time was Captain First Class Sel Janos, a commander from Vojvodina. The commander of the 2nd company was Captain First Class Slobodan Nangelov, a Bulgarian from Dimitrov. Commander of the 3rd Company was Captain Zaim Ajdidovic, a Siptar. If you allow me, I want to say this: When I say "Gypsy" or "a Siptar," I don't mean ill, I just mean an ethnic denomination. The commander of the mortar company was a Gorani. I would not like to mention his name because he and his family may have problems with Siptars in Kosovo and Metohija. Commander of the anti-armour rocket squad was a Macedonian. There was another commander, Dobrica, whose ethnicity I sincerely don't know, Mr. Milosevic, because I never inquired. The main thing for me was that my subordinate commanders execute the orders that they are given and that everything works well. I myself am a Montenegrin. In order to be a Montenegrin, I first have to be a Serb, but I don't want to bother the Trial Chamber with all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So practically all your commanders were of different ethnicities, at least those you enumerated.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all of different ethnicities, but it was one of the best units in the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 66(c) that deals with Mala and Velika Krusa, it says, and we have seen the movement of forces on the map, it says that forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the villages of Mala Krusa and Velika Krusa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct. In order to answer this question, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, I have to explain the difference between the traditional attack as a form of combat operation on the one hand and search of terrain and combat with terrorist forces on the other hand. It would be a very brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it really relevant, necessary? Well, if it's brief, let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain this term "attack" otherwise. In an attack, you have a clearly defined front line, you have clearly defined own forces, supporting forces, and all the other elements. You also know exactly the exact deployment of the enemy, and you use the appropriate forms of manoeuvre to overwhelm the enemy. In this combat action, such as search of terrain and combat with terrorists, there is no classic attack. There is no fire preparation. There is no aviation preparation or rocket preparation. You move the front to search the terrain. When there is no action against the unit, the unit has nothing to respond to and it doesn't act. The moment terrorists start to act or fire, we start to fire, too, to eliminate those firing points. So I cannot accept that there was an attack on Mala and Velika Krusa. It was not an attack. It was solely combat against terrorists who were in that area. And all the villages that I enumerated so far were extremely well fortified. Some of them fortified to the third degree, which implies bunkers and shelters made of reinforced concrete, with barriers over two and a half metres high made of the same material that protects even from a mortar hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as Mala and Velika Krusa are concerned, you're saying that there wasn't an attack but there was some combat action against terrorists who were in the area. That there was some activity there on the part of Serb forces, but it is -- it should not be characterised as an attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I do not accept that the army is a Serbian force, because I just mentioned its ethnic composition. It was a regular unit of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And second, what you said is true: There was no attack in the traditional sense. It was exclusively combat against terrorists. If you mean fire action, there was fire action, which is normally part of every combat activity, but it was exclusively directed at terrorists who opened fire at our troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there is an allegation that the forces of the FRY and Serbia looted and burned -- burnt houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I just said a moment ago that I do not allow for any allegation of that kind that the army of Yugoslavia looted. It is impermissible. It is my duty to speak the truth. I'm an officer, albeit retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is a way in which your witnesses give evidence that is interesting. There is a law that prohibits something, there is a military order or regulation prohibiting something, and your witnesses rely on this as the basis for saying that a particular incident didn't take place. I mean, what a trust we are supposed to have in their fidelity to orders. Your case can't be put in that way. Let us deal with the actual facts. Never mind that it was impermissible, that it is impermissible according to the regulations for them to loot. Did they in fact loot? We wouldn't be here today if -- if there were no breaches of regulations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm afraid there's a small misunderstanding. When the witness says "impermissible," he doesn't mean impermissible according to the law. Of course it's impermissible according to the law. I believe it is an expression of his astonishment at such allegations in the indictment. He simply cannot understand that anybody can claim things like that. That's his point proceeding from what he knows from the ground, from being on the ground at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear his evidence as to what actually happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, could you please just tell us what actually happened on the ground. In what sense did you use the word "impermissible"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I used the word "impermissible" to say that I cannot accept allegations in the indictment of this kind which say that the army of Yugoslavia looted, burnt, and all the other things that are alleged. So if I were to allow that, to permit that and accept that, that means that I would have received an order to do something like that and that I organised something like that, and I'm precisely saying the opposite, that nothing like that happened. If you ask me whether there were individual cases and instances, then we can address individual cases and instances, although not in this area because my unit didn't even have individual cases like that in this particular region. But if we address the rest of the area of responsibility, unfortunately there were instances like that. But then I can also tell you of the measures and steps that I myself took, and I -- and the superior command took to uncover the perpetrators of such crimes and to hand them over to the courts, to the judiciary, to deal with. But as I say, in this part of the country there were no -- even no such incidents, individual incidents. And had anything like that happened, I would, of course, have had to know because it is impossible to cover up things like that in a military organisation, a proper one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, we stopped off discussing the attack on Mala Krusa and Velika Krusa and you said there was no attack. Then in providing us with your explanation, you say how terrains are searched, how you conduct a search of the terrain. And you move across a terrain. When do you open fire?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you exclusively open fire when you are being fired at, when our units were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were moving and only if they shot at you did you shot at the people -- shoot at the people shooting at you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any other circumstance under which you would open fire?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, no other circumstance. That is the kind of action that is undertaken. There are no preventive strikes, as our colleagues from the West like to call them and use the term and concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you just move and open fire only when you're shot at, at the people shooting at you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you explained to us.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to check whether I'd understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the following claims made here, not to mention paragraphs and subparagraphs, I've already mentioned that it's not important as far as you're concerned, but it is claimed that in the morning of the 26th of March, the forces of the FRY and Serbia ordered women and small children to leave the area and go to Albania. And then that they held the men, searched the men, took away their identification papers and valuables and then ordered the men, on threat of death, to move on foot to an uninhabited house in Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would appreciate a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it further states that they forced these men, and it always says the forces of the FRY and Serbia, and the young men to enter the house and that they opened fire at them from a machine-gun --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for a reference. It's paragraph 66(c).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 66(c), yes. I said that at the beginning when I started quoting. I didn't think I needed to specify later on, but here I am repeating: 66(c). On that morning of the 26th of March, they ordered the women and small children to leave the area and go to Albania. They detained and searched the men and boys and confiscated their identity documents and valuables, ordered them to go to a small house in Mala Krusa and then opened fire from a machine-gun, and then they set fire to the house so that the bodies could be burnt. And allegedly during that shooting and in those flames about 105 Kosovo Albanian men and boys died as a result. So there you have it. That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many times I need to repeat that none of this happened. There was no looting. There was no taking of personal documents. There was no confiscating of valuables. And a soldier, generally speaking, cannot loot during the fighting, during combat, even if they wanted to because they wouldn't have anywhere to take the goods, wouldn't know what to do with the goods. All they have is their combat kits and combat kits and rucksacks with a bomb, reserve ammunition, reserve socks, for example, and items of hygiene. So even if anybody wanted to take anything, they wouldn't have anywhere to put it, let alone the fact that there was nowhere any more than ten soldiers without an active commanding officer, and the commanding officer would certainly not have allowed them to engage in any such action. Now, as far as killings are concerned, well, I don't know who could have compiled anything like this because, look, this is what I want to say: If in a closed space you use a machine-gun to shoot, your eardrums would explode. So quite simply this is just not feasible. If I were to analyse each of these allegations, I would see and you would see that something wasn't already there, okay. And I claim, and I was there personally, that this kind of event never took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did anybody die? Did anyone die in the shooting? Because you have acknowledged that your forces would shoot back when you were shot at. So I'm asking, if your forces were shot at and your forces shot back, did anybody die in that shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean terrorists or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, both. You can distinguish them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we take a look at a detailed analysis of the anti-terrorist operation, then you can see losses, casualties on our side, and it is our estimate that, if I remember well, about 80 terrorists, I think was the figure, was killed -- were killed in this anti-terrorist operation. But I must say and I must add this: The bodies of those killed, we rarely came across the bodies of those killed because the terrorists used civilians first and foremost to pull out both the wounded and the killed, their own members who were later secretly buried. So we didn't encounter bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your forces, you're saying, had nothing to do with those who were killed, with the removal of the bodies of those killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: The asanacija or clearing up of the battlefield, asanacija, is an act which is carried out after the fighting has ceased, when there is no combat action and no more danger and no threat to security and safety of one's own unit. And in the order issued by the brigade commander - and I can find it here - in one of the paragraphs of that order, with respect to the rear it says a clearing up of the terrain, of the battlefield. "Asanacija" is the term, and here we have the document. It is point 8(g), clear-up of the battlefield. And this should be done by involving one's own forces and resources once the combat action has ceased in cooperation with the organs and authorities in the territory. Otherwise, Mr. Robinson, for the clear-up of the terrain, we first of all engage civilian structures and teams for clearing up the terrain. They exist attached to the Civil Defence staffs or civilian protection staffs in Prizren, Orahovac, and Djakovica. And the commanders of the military units are duty-bound to locate the spots, to indicate the areas, and to provide support and reinforcement with respect to safety and security for the teams undertaking the clearing up of the terrain in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discovering, uncovering bodies, the bodies of humans and animals and so on. It's a long-lasting process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the asanacija, did your forces collect any of the Albanian bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I answered that question. I said that we didn't encounter any. We didn't come across any, so we didn't collect them up, because this operation went on for four days. We can't interrupt an action, an operation, to pick up the bodies of those killed. And -- but as I said, we didn't come across any bodies because they had been already pulled out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What were your losses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our losses, the loss to my unit was one soldier killed and three wounded, I think. And in the whole brigade, and you can see this from the analysis -- just a moment, I'll find it, that exact spot. I think three dead and seven wounded, but I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for certain about my unit. I can give you the names of the soldiers, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really. What was the size of the terrorist group that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to our estimates, 1.500 terrorists. But on the map -- you can't see it on this map, but if you put the Retimlje map on the overhead projector, then you will be able to see that in the village of Retimlje there was a brigade -- or, rather, the command of the 124th Brigade, if I'm not mistaken but we'll put the map on the overhead projector and then we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't want a map right now. Did you tell us what was the size of your unit, the size of the forces that were involved in the combat action against the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the first and second day, 186 people were engaged, and later on the brigade commander requested that I send another platoon to close off an axis where the terrorists were pulling out towards Mount Milanovac. So my total forces in that operation numbered 220 men. The forces of the army were around 800 and something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us the weapons that your forces used and the weapons used by the -- the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as weapons are concerned, all the weapons that an infantry battalion would generally have, including 120-millimetre mortars which throughout the operation did not shoot a single mine because there was no need to do so. And I was reinforced with a tank platoon and a mechanised platoon - they are combat infantry vehicles - and a platoon of air defence guns, 30-millimetre ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anti-aircraft guns, 30-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the terrorists, they also had excellent weapons, which means they had automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type, most frequently made in China, but they are of the same level. They had excellent sniper rifles, excellent optic sights, produced in the West. They also had light machine-guns, 7.32-millimetres, machine-guns of 7, 9 and 12 millimetres. PKT Russian produced or Browning USA produced. They also had anti-armoured weapons, RPGs or Armbrust, the German type. There was quite a lot of that. They also had recoilless guns, US produced 70 millimetres, and mortars --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did your forces -- did your forces also have machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said they did. We had the weapons that every infantry motorised battalion would have. They are calibres from 7.62 millimetres to 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, may I ask one thing. Is part of your answer, Mr. Vukovic, you said that there was nowhere any more than ten soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving the interpretation. I didn't get what you said. I didn't hear the entire question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vukovic, at one stage in your answer, your last lengthy answer, you said that there was nowhere any more than ten soldiers without an active commanding officer. In what sort of circumstances were groups of that size active without an active commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you. I don't understand your question. An active officer and NCO, they were the commanders of a rifle platoon, for example, numbering 30 men. However, when -- what I said was that the struggle against the terrorists and searching the terrain is a very complex combat operation. Then we tried to take as many officers with us as possible to avoid our own losses and, of course, in order to carry out our assignment as best as possible. And it was in that sense that I said that there were never more than ten -- that an active officer usually was in charge of ten men, talking about the terrorist operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- well, it certainly was not translated that way. It was translated on the basis that ten men might be acting without an active commanding officer. You say that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know what translation you were getting, what interpretation, but I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The next sentence tells that there should be some mistake. If I read the transcript again where you said that ten soldiers, in answer to the question put by the Presiding Judge you said: "So even if anybody wanted to take anything, they wouldn't have anywhere to put it, let alone the fact that there was nowhere any more than ten soldiers without an active commanding officer." And you said, "And the commanding officer would certainly not have allowed them to engage in any such action." So what did you say actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I precisely said what you just read out. That's what I said. I don't know what you wish to hear from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said there's nowhere no more than ten soldiers without an active -- so there should have been a commanding officer. I follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I regret I don't, but perhaps it can be sorted out in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that our forces had taken these people to a house, opened fire, set fire to the house, and that about 105 Kosovo Albanians were killed. And then the names of those killed are set forth in Schedule C. I haven't counted them, but I'm sure that there are probably several dozen of them. They were all male.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have the date of birth of those people, their age?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The average age military-able men, mostly. On the first page, for example -- let me have a look -- there's just one who is 17. I don't want to make a mistake. There is one who is 16 years old. Two are 17 years of age, as far as I can see, but I stand to be corrected. On the second page there's one of 16, one is 15, and one is 13. And on the last page we have one more who is 13, but usually they are 68, 34, 36, 27, 33, 26, 72, 28, 22, et cetera. 23 and so on, 39, 50, 40, 70, 20, 33, and so on and so forth. I'm skipping some. And that's why I said, generally speaking, military-able men have been listed there. From this it emerges that all those who were killed were civilians and that you killed them by collecting them up in a house, executing them, and setting fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. If they were killed, they could have been exclusively killed in battle. They could -- if they were killed, they could only have been killed if they had opened fire and targeted members of the police and army, not outside combat. And I guarantee that. The army never did anything like that. And I can repeat it as many times as you like. And you can bring in all 220 soldiers here who were engaged in that operation with me, and they will confirm it and say the same thing I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any killing of a civilian in that action?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In this action? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any prisoner of the KLA killed?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because you can see from this analysis that nobody was taken prisoner. As for the tactics of Siptar terrorists in Kosovo, I can tell you a lot about after initial failures, after we'd drive them away from well-fortified positions they'd have to abandon, they conceal their weapons or throw them away, they discard their uniforms, change into civilian clothes, and blend with civilians, because they know, they are certain that no repressive measures would be taken against them. In my statements and other statements, you can see that in Brezovac, in addition to lists of terrorists, lists of ammunition, et cetera, we also found parts of military uniforms that belonged to the terrorist organisation of the KLA. As the action proceeds, we find more and more of those uniforms, and we find the most on the last day when they had changed. There was a large group of civilians in Mamusa, and they simply blended with them because they knew the police and army would do nothing against them. That was their tactics in 1998 and, of course, during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, therefore, that they were certain that the army and police would do nothing against civilians.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. That's why they change into civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Ali Hoti, from Velika Krusa, said here that on the 25th of March Serb forces surrounded Velika Krusa village and that he himself had seen tanks and Pragas in the village as well as Serbian forces that had started shelling the village. What can you say about this claim? He testified in April 2002, transcript page 3589.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that it is not true. I have told this story before. The village of Velika Krusa has never been surrounded, one. Second, tanks and Pragas -- it can't be Praga, it must be a 35-millimetre tank. They were never in Velika Krusa, because the police does not dispose of such weapons. Only the army has such weapons. On the road from Prizren to Djakovica or Prizren to Zrze, all up to the 27th, in the evening, there was a blocking unit. Its only task was to not allow the terrorists to run across the Beli Drim river and flee into one the terrorist strongholds; in Rogovo, for instance. But the police did not have such weapons, and they couldn't have gone with them to Velika Krusa. So it's complete nonsense. Allegedly tanks and Pragas, I suppose manned by some people because they can't go in alone, went into the village, and then we ourselves went into the same village, I suppose in order to be shelled by our own. Nonsense. I told you already there was no shelling of Velika Krusa because there was nobody else able to shell apart from my firing group in that terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your own firing group didn't fire a single shell.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. During the entire time of action, that firing group did not fire a single shell. I did have smaller calibres as well, I admit, but there was no shelling of Velika Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, let me just go through your comments on the statement of Ali Hoti, namely that our forces surrounded Velika Krusa. You say it was not surrounded. He claims tanks and Pragas shelled the village. You say there was no shelling at all.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's my assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To that you add the fact that your mortars that were able to shell the village were never used.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Not only then but throughout the four days that my unit or, rather, the part of my unit involved was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness who testified on the 22nd of April, transcript page 3589, says -- his name is Ali Hoti from Velika Krusa. He says that on the 29th of March, 1999, Mehmet Krasniqi told him that on that day in Mala Krusa the Serbian police and paramilitaries rounded up 109 men, including this Krasniqi, took them to a house, covered them with straw, poured petrol on them and set fire to them. This Krasniqi survived somehow. So Ali Hoti learned this from this Krasniqi man.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that none of this is true. There are several untruths in it. It says Serbian police and paramilitaries. Look, concerning paramilitaries, throughout my tour of duty in Kosovo and Metohija I never saw any paramilitaries or, for that matter, any armed member who was not part of the regular units of the army or the police. And I can say with full certainty that Colonel Delic was there. And where he was and where I was, not a single paramilitary soldier could have been for any length of time because he would have been immediately arrested. Then he says they were practically incinerated, poured petrol on and set fire to. There must have been burns. Why didn't this Krasniqi come to show the burns? But there was no rounding up and covering with straw and pouring of petrol and setting fire to. This is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Orahovac municipality there is also the Celine village. You personally were involved in the events in Celine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I and a part of my unit participated in the events or, rather, combat against terrorists in the village of Celine as well. I have already mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under number 11 here, we have a map of Bela Crkva, Celine, 29th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. March, 1999. Sorry, 25th of March. D300, tab 367, admitted through General Delic on the 5th of June -- 5th of July. Could you tell us what happened in Celine on the 25th of March. Where was your unit? What were you doing, pursuant to which order? What were your movements?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On this map we see the deployment of my forces at 1200 hours on the 25th, but I can tell you that in the morning action began from this line that I showed earlier around 0700 hours. Already at 0730 in the area of Celine -- or, rather, from the area of Celine and Velika Krusa, fire was opened at a platoon of mine and a unit of the police that had set out to search the terrain towards Velika Krusa. Combat against fortified terrorists lasted for a little under an hour. We assumed that the greatest part of the terrorists pulled out towards Randubrava village. It was the police unit that entered the village first, because it is their purpose to search populated areas, whereas the army remained on the fringes. After the police conducted the search and established there were no terrorists left in the village, we emerged in our combat disposition on the eastern part of Celine village. You see here the deployment of forces at 1200 hours. In the village of Celine, there was no civilian population before combat operations began, and I've already told you earlier that we were very slow in dealing with these firing tasks precisely because we were not certain whether there were any civilians in the village or not. Later on, during that day and the day after, I ran across groups of civilians, some of which -- some of whom stated that they were natives of Celine and said that they had fled deeper into the territory. As for what I did, I gave specific assignments to my subordinate commanding officers such as to neutralise certain firing positions to protect the troops, to avoid losses among our own troops, and other normal things that every commanding officer does. As for the disposition of units acting towards Celine, that was pursuant to the brigade commander's order to crush the terrorists and to lift the blockade of roads. That is the basis upon which I made my own orders and decisions, adjusting them on the ground to match the developments. As for my unit, you see that emerged on the eastern slopes of Celine village at 1200 hours, and part of the unit was here in Amovac - you can't see it well here - approaching Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have described the course of events up to that point. Is it described in the same way in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been provided here, D300, tab 369, introduced on the 1st of July this year during the testimony of General Delic and at the request of Mr. Nice or, rather, at his objection, it was your ruling that it would only be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, under the next number, 12, is this your statement, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my statement given to the Commission for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal. Of course, in my previous answer I only commented upon the map that is on display, whereas my statement is more detailed. Let me just note that after we passed Celine village, after the completion of combat operations in the village, sometime around 1400 hours - if I could have the map back it would be useful - in the Hoca riverbed we ran into a group of civilians. In my rough estimate there were about 200 of them. One of my commanders found them there, informed me. I went there personally. I talked to them. They were mainly women, children, and elderly men, and I talked to one elderly man. He told me that early in the morning of the 25th, they found shelter there, fleeing Celine and Nogavac to protect themselves from the upcoming action, knowing that there were terrorists in the said villages. He told me, in fact, that the terrorists were not from his village, but they forced them to dig shelters and trenches around the village. I told them -- in fact, I ordered that civilians remain in that area until the army has passed by and then to return to Nogavac because there would be no more action and there were no more terrorists left. I know that at least where Celine is concerned the group reached the village because one of my commanders informed me. I told this commander to change the firing position to avoid any possible incident. And anyway, it was a very small group of soldiers. Only ten soldiers and two commanding officers. For their personal safety, I moved them to the Brinje feature. In the course of the day, we emerged at trig point 450. You can't see it well. There's also trig point 337 that leads to Donje Retimlje. That is where we moved and organised some rest for the troops. And we also made sure that terrorists could not move back or pull out towards the features that we had searched already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this statement, we can see in paragraph 4 what you told us a moment ago, and that is that from the village -- it says: "The first contact with the Siptar terrorist forces was at around 0730 hours when from the area of the Celine village they opened fire on my right flank, platoon right flank on the police units and we responded to the fire. The fighting went on barely an hour when the Siptar forces were routed and probably withdrew to the village of Randubrava." And among other things you say something that you've already said, that: "A police unit searched the village, that I passed by around 10.00 a.m. --" yes, 10.00 a.m., you're quite right -- "and I did not encounter any civilian population." So what you said a moment ago is what you set out here?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph refers to the 200 civilians.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to civilians, don't take these numbers as being final numbers because it's a free estimation. Nobody actually counted them. It was a rough estimate of how many civilians there were, so it might not be the exact figure but give or take. It's a rough estimate. Mine, too, because I was on the spot and also the rough estimate made by my commanders, commanding officers. And we can see that that group later on did leave and went to the village of Celine and went back to their houses. Of course, then came the events of the 1st and 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've already gone through those.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've gone through them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, since this is -- was produced during General Delic's testimony and was just marked for identification, I'd like to tender it into evidence now, this statement by Colonel Vukovic which he has just commented upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've just seen what you gave to the commission. Colonel, just let us dwell for a moment on the statements you made to the Commission for Cooperation. Were you in the expert group?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was not a member of that expert team or commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain how you worked, how you came to give the statements.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was personally contacted by a man whom I happened to know during my years of service earlier on. Colonel Djurovic is his name, and as I say, I had already retired. I was already a retired man when I gave the statement. He told me -- said that we should meet. We did meet, and he explained to me how the commission functioned, what its tasks were, why it was set up in the first place, and he asked me whether I wished to explain the action of my unit at that time and in that location, which I accepted, because it is in my interests to tell the truth about these events, to have the truth be told. So, now, if you mean the actual technique of writing the statement, I wrote it out in longhand and then he typed it out. I looked through his typing, because it was a document, compared it with my original, and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about your subordinate officers? Did they provide the commission with statements as well?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They made statements, those who took part in this operation and those who the expert team managed to find, because some of them had already left the army. That is to say they were no longer in active army service. Another portion was engaged in combat assignments in the security zone, for example, on the ground. So those who were available, he contacted them and they provided him with statements. I have some of those statements here, so if it is of interest to the Court I can read them out too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we might do that. We might take you up on that later on, but do you know that in paragraph 63(a), devoted to Orahovac municipality states that on the morning of the 25th of March, 1999 -- the 25th of March, 1999, is the date, "The forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the village of Celine with tanks and armoured vehicles. After shelling the village, they entered the village and systematically looted and pillaged everything of value from the houses, set houses on shops on fire, and destroyed the old mosque. Because of this, most the Kosovo Albanian villagers fled to a nearby forest before the army and the police arrived."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of strange -- well, if I skip over something, please point that out to me, but let me say that the village of Celine was never surrounded, and no village was during this anti-terrorist operation, if it comes to that. None of the villages were surrounded. There was no reason to surround the village, to surround a village if you want, by your own combat deployment, to do something we refer to as search the terrain. And I claim that the village of Celine was never surrounded. Next, I claim that the -- there was no shelling of the village, and I've already said that. I said that earlier on. Because that group capable of shelling a village did not fire a single shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said you had some reinforcements, a tank platoon or whatever. Did they do any firing perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, there was an order in existence which was given before the war started, and that was that care should be taken and that all calibres should be placed -- the use of all calibre weapons should be placed under control, because we expected to be attacked. So we saved on calibres, on ammunition. And there was no sense in using a tank cannon, for example, a tank gun, to destroy a sniper. So -- as there are other calibres prescribed for that. Now, if you cannot do anything else, then you would use it. However, in the village of Celine, tank weaponry was not used except for a machine-gun, a 7.62-millimetre machine-gun which was positioned on it. Otherwise, permission for the use of tank weapons, a tank cannon, for example, is given exclusively by the brigade command. It is only the brigade commander that can issue such permission. And lower-level commanding officers can only issue orders if a unit is directly attacked, to use armoured vehicles. Next, it says "... systematically looted and pillaged everything of value from the houses." Well, I already said a moment ago that even if a soldier wanted to, he would not have anywhere to put the things that he had taken. Would it be normal to expect that he is shot at carrying a television set on his back, because a television set is a valuable, after all, from a house, let alone any more heavy furniture, items of furniture. Next it says that houses and shops were set on fire. That is absolutely not true. The army never did anything like that. Then it says destroyed the old mosque. I don't remember the old mosque at all. If it was destroyed -- if it is destroyed, then it could only have been destroyed for one reason; because people opened fire from the mosque and targeted the soldiers. And let me remind you if any facility or building is used for military purposes, then it is a legitimate target and may be targeted. I really can't remember the mosque in Celine just now, but I do remember the mosque in Donje Retimlje for sure where there was a sniper and machine-gun nest and for three and a half to four hours they kept us pinned to the ground because we weren't able to advance because of the firing that was very precise and fierce. So even if the mosque was destroyed, it was only destroyed because there was shooting coming from the mosque targeting the army and police. Then it says fled to a nearby forest. Please, around the village of Celine, anybody who doesn't know this area and can't read a map -- or, rather, who can read a map can see that around the village of Celine there is nothing green, which means there are no forests. There are only some orchards, and around the Kocanska river there's something that we call low-lying shrubs, low-lying shrubs of a metre and a half to two metres would be the highest vegetation there. As for a forest, there were no forests in the area. It's all barren. You have forests at Milanovac Mountain, which I mentioned a moment ago, which is at a distance of 10 to 12 kilometres from here. So they couldn't have fled to the nearby forest, as it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They said that they went to a nearby forest even before the army and the police arrived, entered the village.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And I say to you there is no forest there so they could not have fled to a nearby forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this assertion of surrounding a village, you said that there was no surrounding the village.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said there was no shelling of the village.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Looting, what about looting?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said, right, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't any?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. If you ask me whether there were any destroyed houses, there were but only in this respond to the firepower from the terrorists. But intentional burning, that certainly didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's another example, Colonel. If there was any -- any destroyed houses, it was only in response to the firepower from the terrorists. But, I mean, can you state as a matter of fact that this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was the position, that there was firepower from the terrorists and in returning the firepower -- in returning fire, houses were destroyed? I mean, that is what is important to us as evidence, what happened as a matter of fact, not what ought to have happened on the basis of the orders by which your forces are supposed to operate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I've just been saying are just facts, and I'm telling you this on the basis of my own personal experience. I was there throughout the time, in the first front line with my soldiers. So everything that I'm telling you is fact. Now, if you take a look otherwise at the axis of where my unit was operational, the entire village of Celine is halfway -- is in the middle of the width of that zone. So I was personally physically present in the village of Celine, if that's what you mean, so I'm just telling you of the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you did see houses destroyed? You were a witness to the destruction of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not an eyewitness to the destruction of houses. I'm telling you -- what I'm saying is that there were individual houses which were destroyed but only as the result of the effects of weapons and in destroying the fire positions -- firing positions of the terrorists that were targeting us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were a witness to the destruction of these individual houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a witness. In every war there is destruction of houses. You have houses destroyed in every war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not on the basis of supposition and what happens in every war. What happened on the day when you were there? Are you saying that you witnessed the destruction of individual houses; and secondly, are you saying that that was done as a response to fire from the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the transcript, things will be clearer. So there was -- they opened fire from a number of houses that were prepared to be fired from, which means on the windows you would have sacks filled with -- sandbags and sacks filled with earth. There was -- were windows and doors knocked down on the other side so that they could shoot from the house, because if you fire a high calibre bullet from a closed-in house, then your eardrums would explode. So the village of Celine was a fortification of that kind, and as a result, these firing points were destroyed when they were in houses. So my answer is yes, I was present when individual houses which were used by the terrorists were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps that clarifies it, but you've just a short while before said you weren't present. You are assuring us that you saw it actually happen and that you didn't simply see the results of what had happened earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what results you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By "results" I mean the damage. You're not simply saying, "I saw the damage later." Are you actually saying that you saw the damage being done by the firing by your forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear, that you see it straight away. If you shoot at the enemy in a house, of course the house is damaged, and that is -- you can see that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you actually see that happening? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. This is quite clear. Just let me take a look at what it says further on. That same paragraph, for the benefit of the interpreters, who have the document in front of them, I'd like to draw their attention that I'm still dealing with paragraph 63(a). Towards the end of that paragraph, it says: "On the 28th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia forced the thousands of people hiding in the forest to come out. After marching the civilians to a nearby village, the men were separated from the women and were beaten, robbed, and all their identity documents were taken from them. The men were then marched to Prizren and eventually forced to go to Albania." There you have it. That's what it says in paragraph (a).

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely not correct. First of all, on the 28th of March -- and I assume that this paragraph relates to Celine, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The army was -- my unit specifically was in Retimlje, Donje Retimlje, and part of Mamusa. So on that 28th, Mr. Milosevic, my unit was not operational at all. It didn't go into action at all. We were just replenishing our forces; fuel, gathering up our soldiers and preparing to march to the village of Bistrazin. So on the 28th, there were absolutely no soldiers. And even these forces who were in the blockade, on the 27th returned to their own areas. So there were no soldiers there on the 28th. There were no soldiers in this area here on the 28th of March. Now, as for forcible taking of identity documents and so on, I state that none of that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean none of that happened there or none of that happened anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in my unit that never happened. And I think that individual cases of abuse and individual cases of crimes can be addressed. I can tell you of individual examples when you ask me, but not here; they didn't happen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A witness of the opposite side, Reshit Salihi, from the village of Celine, said that on the 24th of March the Serb army was wearing black uniforms and that it opened fire on houses and buildings including the mosque in Celine and that on that occasion they set fire to the houses or, rather, that the units of the army of Yugoslavia that day surrounded the village of Celine, shelled it, set fire to it, and then the army entered the village and that's when they opened fire and shot at the houses and buildings there. And he testified from the 19th to the 22nd of April, 19 -- 2002. This is page 3542 of the transcript. Therefore, he says that on the 24th of April, the army was there in black uniforms, that they opened fire and shot at the mosque, that they set fire to the houses, surrounded the village, shelled it, and then entered the village and opened fire and shot at the houses and buildings.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This does not correspond to the truth. On the 24th of March, my unit was in a village called Zup. It was not in Celine at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us assume that he made a mistake about that.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As for black uniforms, the only black uniforms in Kosovo and Metohija were worn by terrorists, members of the terrorist so-called Kosovo Liberation Army. In our ranks, or in the ranks the Ministry of the Interior, I have never seen a black uniform. And incidentally, these black uniforms are appearing in Kosovo, in Metohija these days. At least, that's what the media report. As for his statement that the army opened fire inside houses, it's complete nonsense. To open fire on empty buildings, not a single soldier, not a single unit would do that, because among other things, for every mission a certain amount of ammunition is approved to be spent. What are we to do, to spend all our ammunition recklessly and then remain without any when we face terrorists eventually? Complete nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness says that men were separated from women and children, men were robbed, their ID papers taken away, and later on the men formed a line at gunpoint, walking to Prizren, and that at one point they stood for six hours with their arms above their heads. That's what he testified. I have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already spoken about this group of civilians. It's not true that anybody took anything away from them, that they were robbed of their valuables and ID papers. We didn't even check their papers. I don't see any purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Colonel. You said that in some riverbed you found a group of about 200 civilians, but what he says concerns Celine. He says that an army unit entered the village that day, that they separated men from women and children, and then robbed men of valuables and papers and marched them in columns.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already told you, Mr. Milosevic, that in Celine village there had been no civilian population before combat operations began. I learned this from civilians who were hiding in the Hoca riverbed. They told me themselves. And later on when we entered the village, we established for ourselves that there were no civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness says that on the 26th of March, around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, a group of over 40 policemen reached Pisjak [phoen] woods where 5 to 6.000 refugees were hiding and, under threat, took away their valuables and identification papers. What can you say about that? 26 March in the morning.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To say the least, it sounds illogical, because he said earlier that on the 24th we drove them away towards Prizren. Then how were we able to find them on the 26th in some woods if we had already driven them away towards Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that he got that wrong. Where was your unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning on the 26th, my unit was already approaching Randubrava and the search of that village was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is this Pisjak woods?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know honestly. It's not on the map. I suppose it's some local name. But I keep telling you one thing: There is no woods in this area. There are only orchards, vineyards, and trees here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it possible for 5 to 6.000 people to hide in those orchards and vineyards? Is it possible for 40 policemen to come there, rob them of money, valuables, and ID papers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's simply impossible for such a large group to be in one area without being seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th, were you in the area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was, Mr. Milosevic. I have been telling you where I was from the 25th until 28th. I was in that area. And a large concentration of refugees was only in Mamusa village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the Turkish village?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's populated mainly by Turks. And at least twice as many civilians were there from the neighbouring villages. On the 28th, I spoke to the locals of Mamusa, and I can tell you that they did not want to buy weapons from terrorists, because the terrorists used to sell weapons to their own people under very serious threats, at very high prices. The Mamusa people did not want any of that, and they were maltreated by terrorists. And the Mamusa people complained they simply couldn't cope with such a large number of people in their village. They had nowhere to put them up. But to speak of such a large number of people hiding anywhere, it's simply not true. I told you, we came across groups of 100, 200 - in one case there were 500 - but never more, except in Mamusa village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The issue of how many people could have been in a group is one thing. Did anybody mistreat these people, take anything away from them, rob them, even if there were only 15? Did anybody separate men from women?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The army never looted, robbed, separated men from women or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Agim Zeqiri, another witness, says there was a convoy of refugees escorted by army and police of Yugoslavia, numbering about 4.000 people, moving towards Albania. Was there a convoy that was gathered in Orahovac? Was anybody directing it towards Albania? Did anybody drive away these people and make them go to Albania, as witnesses say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Even if that convoy existed, it was certainly not escorted by the army. As far as I know, it wasn't escorted by the police either. It's true that after the aggression began on the 24th of March, and especially on the 25th and throughout the first days of April, there was a lot of civilians who were going to Albania. They could have gone to central Serbia or Montenegro, but for reasons known only to them, most of them decided to go to Albania, but the convoys were never escorted or directed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell them to leave their homes and go?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. Whenever we had contact with them, we told them to stay in their villages, not to leave. If that's what you're asking me, my answer is that there was no attempt to persuade them or to order them to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Jusuf Jemini from Celine - he could be Jemini or Jemini, I'm not sure about the pronunciation, but from Celine - he testified on the 24th of July, transcript 8559. He says in his testimony that over the radio code 444 he heard a conversation between a policeman from Celine who was saying that many people had been killed in Celine whereas the other voice asked him, "Is it a larger massacre than in Racak?" And the first one answered, "It's twice as big." Now, what can you tell us about this massacre in Celine? The statement of that witness was exhibited under number 276.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This massacre in Celine is non-existent, and I'm slightly confused by this code 444, and I'm confused by how come a civilian can have a radio device that is only used by police or army. And if he had a radio device, how did he stumble upon the frequency used by the army or the police? I'm absolutely -- I'm almost certain that in this operation we had a code name Poljanica, and to this name Poljanica a certain number was added for purposes of identification during calls. Although we could tell each other's voice even without those code names. As for the police, I believe their code name for the operation was Cegan, plus a certain number. So this code is a fiction. I told you I was in Celine and my unit was in Celine and there was no massacre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said there was no civilian population as such in Celine.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only in the 20 -- in the afternoon of the 25th, part of the civilians were told to return to the village after the completion of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just find this number.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under number 18, we have your statement, a statement that you gave in relation to the events from the 25th to the 28th of March.
